title: The Gene: An Intimate History
author: Siddhartha Mukherjee
description: Starts with Mukherjee's Bengali family mystery in Kolkata, jumps straight to the 3D DNA double-helix discovery, hops back to Mendel's pea packets, and closes with Epigenetics & Identity.

adhd_segments.label: Step 1 · Prologue: Families in Kolkata (Start Here — The Personal Mystery)
adhd_segments.brief: Siddhartha Mukherjee travels with his father through Kolkata to visit his schizophrenic cousin Moni, asking how a tiny physical code inside our cells carries both brilliance and mental illness across generations.

adhd_segments.label: Step 2 · Jumps to Part II: Seeing the 3D DNA Double Helix (Franklin, Crick & Watson)
adhd_segments.brief: Jumps ahead to 1953 Cambridge and London, where Rosalind Franklin's X-ray photographs and Watson and Crick's brass models reveal the physical four-letter twisted staircase that copies all life.

adhd_segments.label: Step 3 · Jumps Back to Part I: Mendel's Pea Garden (How Discrete Code Packets Work)
adhd_segments.brief: Now that you can picture DNA, we jump back to Gregor Mendel cross-breeding 28,000 pea plants in his monastery garden to prove that traits pass from parent to child as unbreakable packets rather than blended fluids.

adhd_segments.label: Step 4 · Jumps to Epilogue: Bheda, Abheda (Epigenetics, Fate & Human Freedom)
adhd_segments.brief: Returns to the Mukherjee family and the modern CRISPR era, showing how environmental triggers flip genetic switches on and off and why understanding our genome liberates us from fatalism.

author_chapters.label: Prologue: Families
author_chapters.brief: A personal journey into the Mukherjee family history of schizophrenia in Kolkata and the central question of heredity.

author_chapters.label: Part I: The Missing Science of Heredity (1865–1935)
author_chapters.brief: Aristotle, Darwin's pangenesis puzzle, Mendel's monastery pea experiments, and the dark detour of early eugenics.

author_chapters.label: Part II: In the Sum of the Parts (1930–1970)
author_chapters.brief: Morgan's fruit-fly room, Oswald Avery's transformation experiment, and the discovery of the DNA double helix.

author_chapters.label: Part III: The Dreams of Geneticists (1970–2001)
author_chapters.brief: Genetic engineering, recombinant DNA, cloning genes, and the birth of modern biotechnology.

author_chapters.label: Part IV: The Proper Study of Mankind Is Man (1970–2005)
author_chapters.brief: Hunting disease genes across human families and the global race to map the entire human genome.

author_chapters.label: Part V: Through the Looking Glass (2001–2015)
author_chapters.brief: The biology of identity, race, gender, intelligence, temperament, and epigenetic switches.

author_chapters.label: Part VI: Post-Genome & Epilogue: Bheda, Abheda
author_chapters.brief: CRISPR gene editing, embryonic diagnosis, and the philosophical synthesis of difference and sameness.

title: The Man Who Knew Infinity
author: Robert Kanigel
description: Opens right at the electric 1913 Cambridge letter to G. H. Hardy, flashes back to Ramanujan's South Indian temple slates, jumps to his clash with Hardy over proof vs. intuition, and finishes with 1729 & Mock Theta functions.

adhd_segments.label: Step 1 · Jumps to Ch. 4: The 1913 Letter That Stunned G. H. Hardy (Start Here)
adhd_segments.brief: Starts at the dramatic turning point in January 1913 when Cambridge mathematician G. H. Hardy opens a messy envelope from an unknown Madras clerk and realizes these wild infinite series could only come from a genius.

adhd_segments.label: Step 2 · Flashes Back to Prologue & Ch. 1–2: Temple Porch & Carr's Book in Kumbakonam
adhd_segments.brief: Flashes back to South India along the Kaveri River, showing how young Ramanujan worked out thousands of theorems on an elbow-rubbed slate on his porch, experiencing formulas as direct visions from Goddess Namagiri.

adhd_segments.label: Step 3 · Jumps to Ch. 6: Flint and Stone — Pure Intuition Meets Rigorous Proof
adhd_segments.brief: Inside Trinity College, Ramanujan's lightning-fast pattern intuition collides with Hardy's insistence on formal step-by-step proof, producing their breakthrough formula for integer partitions.

adhd_segments.label: Step 4 · Jumps to Ch. 8: Taxicab 1729 & Mock Theta Functions
adhd_segments.brief: Even while ill in Putney and returning to Madras, Ramanujan instantly spots 1729 as the smallest sum of two cubes in two ways and writes down mock theta functions now used in black-hole physics.

author_chapters.label: Prologue
author_chapters.brief: Mahalanobis in Cambridge and the legend of Srinivasa Ramanujan's leap from South India to Trinity College.

author_chapters.label: Ch. 1: In the Shadow of the Temple (1887–1903)
author_chapters.brief: Kumbakonam childhood, Brahmin upbringing, and early mathematical prodigy before discovering Carr's book.

author_chapters.label: Ch. 2: Ranging with Delight (1903–1908)
author_chapters.brief: Carr's Synopsis sets Ramanujan's mind on fire; he fails college exams because he will only do mathematics.

author_chapters.label: Ch. 3: The Search for Patrons (1908–1913)
author_chapters.brief: Marriage to Janaki, poverty in Madras, showing his frayed notebooks door-to-door, and clerkship at the Port Trust.

author_chapters.label: Ch. 4: Hardy (up to 1913)
author_chapters.brief: G. H. Hardy's life at Cambridge and the morning Ramanujan's nine-page letter of theorems arrives.

author_chapters.label: Ch. 5: 'I Beg to Introduce Myself' (1913–1914)
author_chapters.brief: Neville travels to Madras, Goddess Namagiri grants permission in a dream, and Ramanujan sails from India.

author_chapters.label: Ch. 6: Ramanujan's Spring (1914–1916)
author_chapters.brief: Collaborating with Hardy and Littlewood at Cambridge on highly composite numbers and partitions.

author_chapters.label: Ch. 7: The English Chill (1916–1918)
author_chapters.brief: Wartime food shortages, illness, election as Fellow of the Royal Society and Trinity College.

author_chapters.label: Ch. 8: Return to the Cauvery & Epilogue (1918–1920)
author_chapters.brief: Homecoming to India, final notebooks on mock theta functions, and enduring legacy across modern math.

adhd_segments.label: Step 4 · Jumps to Ch. 10 & 12: Meeting Sri Yukteswar & Serampore Training

adhd_segments.label: Step 5 · Jumps Back to Ch. 1–2: Bengali Parents, Childhood & Mother's Amulet

author_chapters.label: Ch. 4–7: Himalayan Flight, Tiger Swami & The Levitating Saint

author_chapters.label: Ch. 14–16: Cosmic Consciousness, Cauliflower Robbery & Outwitting the Stars
author_chapters.brief: Samadhi awakening and Sri Yukteswar's fierce lessons on deeper law over superstition.

author_chapters.brief: Travels with Sri Yukteswar to Kashmir and graduating from Scottish Church College.

title: Fundamentals of Biostatistics
author: Bernard Rosner
description: Starts with Ch. 3 (Bayes' Theorem & medical screening intuition), jumps to Ch. 5–6 (Central Limit Theorem), hops back to Ch. 1–2 (Descriptive Spread), and finishes with Ch. 7 (Hypothesis Testing & P-Values).

adhd_segments.label: Step 1 · Jumps to Ch. 3: Bayes' Theorem & Real-World Medical Screening (Start Here)
adhd_segments.brief: Starts with the most counter-intuitive puzzle in statistics: why a 99% accurate clinical test still produces mostly false alarms on a rare condition, and how Bayes' rule calculates the real probability.

adhd_segments.label: Step 2 · Jumps to Ch. 5–6: Normal Distribution & The Central Limit Theorem
adhd_segments.brief: Shows visually why averaging noisy biological measurements always converges into a clean bell curve, allowing small clinical samples to predict population truth.

adhd_segments.label: Step 3 · Jumps Back to Ch. 1–2: Center vs. Spread (Mean, Median & Variance)
adhd_segments.brief: Returns to the foundations to show how skewed real-world numbers fool simple averages and how variance and interquartile range capture the true spread.

adhd_segments.label: Step 4 · Jumps to Ch. 7: Hypothesis Testing, P-Values & Statistical Power
adhd_segments.brief: Unpacks the physical meaning of null hypotheses, Type I false alarms vs. Type II misses, and how to tell real treatment effect from luck.

author_chapters.label: Ch. 2: Descriptive Statistics

author_chapters.label: Ch. 3: Probability

author_chapters.label: Ch. 4: Discrete Probability Distributions

author_chapters.label: Ch. 5: Continuous Probability Distributions

author_chapters.label: Ch. 6: Estimation
author_chapters.brief: Sampling distributions, Central Limit Theorem, and confidence intervals.

author_chapters.label: Ch. 7–8: Hypothesis Testing (One-Sample & Two-Sample)
author_chapters.brief: t-tests, p-values, statistical power, and sample-size determination.

author_chapters.label: Ch. 9–10: Nonparametric & Categorical Data Methods
author_chapters.brief: Rank tests, contingency tables, and chi-square tests.

author_chapters.label: Ch. 11–14: Regression, Correlation, ANOVA & Survival Analysis
author_chapters.brief: Linear/logistic regression, multivariable models, and Kaplan-Meier survival curves.

title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
author: Daniel Kahneman
description: Starts with Ch. 1–2 (System 1 vs. System 2), jumps straight to the end (Ch. 35: Experiencing vs. Remembering Self), hops to Part IV (Ch. 26: Prospect Theory & Loss Aversion), then Ch. 5 (Cognitive Ease), and Ch. 11 (Anchoring).

adhd_segments.label: Step 1 · Ch. 1–2: Fast System 1 vs. Effortful System 2 (Start Here)
adhd_segments.brief: Introduces the two actors inside your brain: automatic System 1 that builds instant visual movies, and lazy, energy-protective System 2 that avoids heavy cognitive load.

adhd_segments.label: Step 2 · Jumps to Part V (Ch. 35–36): The Experiencing Self vs. The Remembering Self
adhd_segments.brief: Jumps to Kahneman's deepest life insight: why the self that lives in the present moment is completely different from the storyteller self that judges experiences only by their peak and their ending.

adhd_segments.label: Step 3 · Jumps Back to Part IV (Ch. 26): Prospect Theory & Loss Aversion
adhd_segments.brief: Unpacks the Nobel Prize discovery of why losing ₹1,000 triggers twice as much gut pain as winning ₹1,000 brings joy, and how reference points govern human risk.

adhd_segments.label: Step 4 · Jumps Back to Part I (Ch. 5): Cognitive Ease & Why Familiarity Feels True
adhd_segments.brief: Shows how clear typography, simple language, and a calm mood put System 1 into 'Cognitive Ease,' lowering your guard and making everything feel effortless and true.

adhd_segments.label: Step 5 · Jumps to Part II (Ch. 11 & 17): Anchoring & Regression to the Mean
adhd_segments.brief: Reveals how arbitrary numbers silently hijack negotiations and why unusually good or bad days naturally revert toward average without needing a causal story.

author_chapters.brief: Origins of Kahneman and Amos Tversky's collaboration on intuition and bias.

author_chapters.label: Part I: Two Systems (Ch. 1–9)
author_chapters.brief: System 1 and System 2, attention and effort, associative memory, cognitive ease, and jumping to conclusions.

author_chapters.label: Part II: Heuristics and Biases (Ch. 10–18)
author_chapters.brief: Law of small numbers, anchors, availability cascades, base-rate neglect, and regression to the mean.

author_chapters.label: Part III: Overconfidence (Ch. 19–24)
author_chapters.brief: The narrative fallacy, illusion of validity, algorithms vs. intuition, and the outside view.

author_chapters.label: Part IV: Choices (Ch. 25–34)
author_chapters.brief: Bernoulli's errors, Prospect Theory, the endowment effect, sunk-cost traps, and mental accounting.

author_chapters.label: Part V: Two Selves & Conclusions (Ch. 35–38)
author_chapters.brief: Experiencing self vs. remembering self, peak-end rule, and life satisfaction.
